```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
workdir <- file.path(tempdir(), "agents-article")
dir.create(workdir, showWarnings = FALSE)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = workdir)
ri <- function(x) knitr::inline_expr(x)
```

This article is for authors who let a coding agent, such as Claude Code,
edit a weft project, and for the agents themselves. After it you will know
what weft tells an agent, why, and how each kind of finding should be
answered.

## Why an agent needs rules

weft's checks fail on purpose. A failed claim says that the prose and the
numbers disagree. The commit gate refuses a typed number. Removing a
construct needs a line in the commit message.

An agent asked to "make the render pass" has easy ways to do it that defeat
the point: loosen the claim, delete the check, type the number back in as a
literal, turn on draft mode, or commit with `--no-verify`. Each makes the
error go away and leaves the report wrong. The rules below close those
ways, and say what to do instead.

## What `use_agent_docs()` writes

`use_agent_docs()` writes an `AGENTS.md` block and a skill. `use_weft()` runs it, or you can run
it alone (see `vignette("setup", package = "weft")`).

The first is a block in `AGENTS.md`, the file many coding agents read when
they start. weft appends it after any text already there:

```{r, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(system.file("agent", "AGENTS.md", package = "weft")), sep = "\n")
```

In the project, the block sits between a `<!-- weft:start ... -->` line and
a `<!-- weft:end -->` line. weft replaces only what lies between them.
Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, not `AGENTS.md`. If the project has a
`CLAUDE.md`, add the line `@AGENTS.md` to it so that it includes the block.

The second is a skill, `weft/SKILL.md`, which a coding agent loads when a
task touches a weft document or a weft report. It sits in each skills folder
(see the next section), with two files in `references/`, `syntax.md` and
`reports.md`:

```{r, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(system.file("agent", "SKILL.md", package = "weft")), sep = "\n")
```

In the project, the placeholders (the version in `metadata` and the last
line, and the hash) hold the weft version and a hash, so that `use_agent_docs()` can tell whether you have edited the
file.

## Which tools read which folder: `skills`

The skill format is the same for every tool; the tools differ in the folder
they scan. `use_agent_docs(skills = )` takes preset names or folders relative
to the project root, and writes the same files into each:

| preset | folder | read by |
|---|---|---|
| `agents` | `.agents/skills` | Gemini CLI; reported for Codex, opencode and Cursor |
| `claude` | `.claude/skills` | Claude Code |
| `codex` | `.agents/skills` | reported for Codex |
| `gemini` | `.gemini/skills` | Gemini CLI |
| `opencode` | `.opencode/skills` | reported for opencode |
| `kimi` | `.kimi-code/skills` | Kimi Code |
| `cursor` | `.cursor/skills` | reported for Cursor |

The default is `c("agents", "claude")`. That Codex, opencode and Cursor read
`.agents/skills` is reported by secondary sources; it was not checked against
the vendors' documents. A folder of your own is a path such as
`"tools/skills"`; an absolute path or one with `..` is an error.
`skills = character()` writes only the `AGENTS.md` block. Gemini CLI reads
`GEMINI.md`, so if the project has one, add the line `@AGENTS.md` to it; the
call says so.

The copies in a project can be older than the installed package.
`weft::agent_docs()` lists the documents and `weft::agent_docs("syntax")`
prints the installed version of one.

## The four rules

### A failed claim is a finding, not an error

When a claim fails, the sentence, the check and the value disagree. One of
them is wrong, and only the author knows which. Here a draft says all
sites met the guideline, and one did not:

```{r}
writeLines(c(
  "---",
  "title: \"Survey\"",
  "output: md_document",
  "knitr:",
  "  opts_knit:",
  "    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()",
  "---",
  "",
  "```{r data}",
  "ntu <- c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 12.6)",
  "```",
  "",
  "All sites were below the guideline, with a highest reading of `r claim(max(ntu), . < 10)`."
), "survey.Rmd")
r <- tryCatch(rmarkdown::render("survey.Rmd", quiet = TRUE),
              error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
```

The agent should report this to the author, with its reading of which part
looks wrong. Here the data look right, so the sentence is wrong. It should
not:

- change the check to `. < 15`;
- delete the `claim()`;
- edit the data to fit.

The author may still choose any of these. The rule is that the agent does
not choose for them.

### Do not change a check to make something pass

A **check** is a `claim()`, an `if` guard on a span, or a bound such as the
one in `. < 10`. Removing or loosening one to clear a failure needs the
author's explicit request for exactly that change.

### Removed constructs carry the trailer

When a commit removes weft constructs on purpose, the hook prints the
number to declare:

```text
  or commit with: git commit --trailer "Weft-Removed: 2"
```

The agent adds that trailer, with that number. It does not use
`git commit --no-verify` to get past the hook. A wrong number is refused.

### A chapter's own values go in `dict_local`

A value that holds for one document goes in that document's front matter,
with a `why`:

```yaml
weft:
  dict_local:
    lab_sites:
      value: 4
      type: number
      definition: "Sites sent to the laboratory in this chapter."
      why: "Only the autumn survey sent samples away."
```

It is read as `` `r ri("dict_local$lab_sites")` ``. A value two documents
need belongs in `dict.yml` (see `vignette("units", package = "weft")`).

## Answering each kind of finding

The gate and `lints()` name each finding by its rule. This table says how
to answer the common ones.

| Finding | Answer |
|---|---|
| `numeral`: a number typed in prose | Compute it and write `` `r ri("x")` ``. If it is a choice, put it in `dict.yml` and write `` `r ri("dict$key")` ``. If it is quoted from a source, put it in a `cite` span. Only a number that is fixed by something outside the analysis, such as a method's pore size, becomes `[0.45 µm]{.weft-literal why="..."}`, with a `why` that says what fixes it. |
| `numeral` on "Site 4" | The number is a name. Ask the author to add the word to `label_words` in `_weft.yml`. |
| `numeral` on "Figure 2" | Write a cross-reference, such as `@fig-map`. |
| `literal-value`: a value made of constants, such as `` `r ri("3 + 4")` `` | Compute it from data, or treat it as a typed number. |
| `construct`: weft syntax that does not parse | Fix the syntax. The message names the rule broken. |
| constructs removed | If intended, add the `Weft-Removed: N` trailer. If not, put them back. |
| failed claim | Report it to the author. Do not edit the check or the value. |
| `xref`, `anchor-twice` | Add the missing anchor, or rename the duplicate. |
| `section-anchor` | Add `{#sec-name}` to the heading. |
| `chunk-label` | Add `#| label: name` to the chunk. |
| `figure` | Add the label, caption or alt text the message names. |
| `engine` | Add `engine: knitr` to the document's own front matter. |
| `dict-key` | Use a key that `dict.yml` holds, or ask the author to add the entry. |

A `.weft-literal` whose `why` is "fixed", "needed" or "to pass the check"
is a typed number with a label. The `why` is the only record of the
decision, so it must say something a reader can check.

`vignette("lints", package = "weft")` describes every rule.

## Draft mode is not a way through

`draft: true` in `_weft.yml`, or `WEFT_DRAFT=1`, makes a render report its
failures and finish. It is for an author part-way through a chapter. An
agent should not turn it on to get a render to finish, and should not
leave a project in it. `verify()` refuses to run in draft mode, so the
project cannot be checked until it is off. The commit gate still runs.

## Before committing, and before handing back

- **Before a commit**, run `weft::lints()`. It lists the findings in the
  project. Those that the last commit did not hold are the ones the hook
  will refuse. `weft::gate()` judges what is staged exactly as the hook
  will.
- **Before handing work back**, run `weft::verify()`. It renders every
  document and checks every claim. A failure there is a finding to report.
- **Read `weft::changes()`** after a render, and tell the author about each
  structural change and each new condition. Those are the places where a
  sentence elsewhere may now be wrong.
